essays.stem: Explain what 'coordinating materials' means for the team leader on a fabrication job, and describe who he must work with to do it well.
essays.modelAnswer: Coordinating materials means making sure the right steel, consumables, gases, paint and bought-in parts are in the right place, in the right amount and condition, at the right time, and that their use is tracked. It starts with working out what the job needs from the drawings, then planning when each item must arrive, checking it when it comes, storing it safely, issuing it to the welders, watching how it is used and dealing with offcuts, surplus and scrap at the end. The team leader must work with the drawing office or estimator for the bill of materials, with purchasing for orders and delivery dates, with the stores for stock, receiving and issue, with the welders and fitters for what they need and when, with the inspector for certificates and traceability, and with the manager on costs and problems. He keeps everyone informed when plans change.
markingPoints: Right materials, amount, condition, place and time
Covers the stages: requirements, scheduling, receiving, storage, issue, use, surplus
Works with drawing office/estimator and purchasing
Works with stores, welders and the inspector
Keeps the manager and others informed when plans change

essays.stem: Describe how you would work out all the materials needed for a steel staircase from its drawings, and plan when each must be in the shop.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the approved drawings and list every part: stringers, treads, landings, posts, handrails, base plates, cleats and bolts. For each I would note the section, size, grade and number off, to make a bill of materials. I would plan how the parts come out of standard lengths and sheets to keep waste low, and add an allowance for offcuts. Then I would add consumables: electrodes or wire, gas, grinding and cutting discs, primer and paint, worked out from the weld lengths and areas. I would check the store first and mark what is already in stock. Next I would match each item to the programme: plate and stringer sections are needed first for cutting, then the posts and rails, while paint is only needed near the end. I would allow for each supplier's lead time and any galvanising, and set the date each item must arrive. I would give the schedule to purchasing and the store and keep it up to date.
markingPoints: Lists every part from the drawings with section, size, grade and quantity (bill of materials)
Plans cutting from standard lengths and allows for waste
Adds consumables, gases and paint
Checks existing stock first
Matches arrival dates to the programme and lead times; shares the schedule

essays.stem: Explain how you would keep material traceability on a job that needs mill certificates, from receiving the steel to the finished item.
essays.modelAnswer: When the steel arrives, I would check that each length or plate has a heat number stamped or painted on it and that the number matches a mill certificate showing the right grade. The certificates would be kept in the job file. The steel would be stored apart from general stock and labelled with the job number. Before any cutting, the heat number and job number would be transferred to every piece that will be cut off, including offcuts that go back to the rack, with a paint marker or low-stress stamp. A cutting record would list each part mark against its heat number. Welding consumables would also be recorded by batch. As the item is assembled, the inspector checks the marks before welding hides them, and the record is updated. At the end, the job file shows each part, its heat number and certificate, so the client or inspector can trace any part back to the mill.
markingPoints: Checks heat numbers against mill certificates on arrival; files certificates
Stores certified steel apart, labelled with the job
Transfers heat and job numbers to every piece, and offcuts, before cutting
Keeps a cutting record and consumable batch records
Final job file links every part to its certificate

essays.stem: Describe how steel sections, plate, welding consumables and gas cylinders should each be stored in a fabrication shop, and say why.
essays.modelAnswer: Steel sections and bar should be stored on racks or timber bearers, off the ground and under cover where possible, sorted by size and grade and labelled, so they stay dry, do not bend and are easy to find. Plate is best stored on edge in a plate rack or flat on bearers with packing between sheets, so it can be lifted safely with a clamp. Stainless and aluminium must be kept apart from carbon steel so that dust does not contaminate them. Electrodes and wire are kept in a dry store in their sealed packs; opened low-hydrogen electrodes go in a holding oven, as the maker says, because moisture causes porosity and cracking. Gas cylinders are stored upright and chained, in a ventilated, shaded store, with oxygen kept apart from fuel gases such as acetylene, full cylinders apart from empties, and valve caps on, to reduce the risk of fire and falling cylinders. Paint and thinners go in a separate ventilated store, away from hot work.
markingPoints: Sections on racks or bearers, off the ground, sorted and labelled
Plate stored for safe lifting; stainless and aluminium kept apart
Consumables dry and sealed; low-hydrogen electrodes in an oven
Cylinders upright, chained, ventilated, oxygen apart from fuel gas, full apart from empty
Gives reasons (rust, damage, finding stock, fire, safety)

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the safe handling and moving of long steel lengths and large plates around the shop and onto a truck.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would work out the mass of each load from its size, for example a 10 mm plate of 1.5 m by 1 m is about 118 kg, too heavy to carry by hand. I would choose the right equipment: the overhead crane or a hoist with a plate clamp for plates, and two slings or a lifting beam near each end for long lengths so they stay level. All lifting gear must be inspected, tagged and have a safe working load above the load. Only trained people would operate the crane or forklift, with one person giving signals. I would plan the route, clear it, and keep people out from under the load. Tag lines would be used to steady long lengths. On the truck, the load would be placed on bearers, in the order it will be unloaded, and strapped down so it cannot slide or roll. Workers would wear gloves, boots and hard hats, and nobody would ride on a load or the forks.
markingPoints: Works out the mass and avoids manual handling of heavy loads
Chooses suitable lifting equipment and checks SWL and inspection tags
Trained operators, one signaller, cleared route, nobody under the load
Tag lines and level lifts for long lengths
Truck loaded on bearers in order and strapped down; PPE worn

essays.stem: Describe how you would issue materials to welders on a busy job and keep track of what is used.
essays.modelAnswer: I would issue materials against the job's bill of materials and cutting list, not on request alone. For each assembly, the store would prepare a kit: the cut parts, bolts and the right consumables, in a tray or stillage marked with the job and assembly numbers. Each issue would be recorded on an issue note with the job number, the item, the quantity and the welder's signature, and the bin cards would be updated. Consumables such as electrodes, wire, discs and gas would be issued in the amounts needed for a day or a shift, with low-hydrogen electrodes in a heated quiver. Unused items and offcuts would come back to the store at the end of the day and be booked back. Each week I would compare what was issued with the estimate and the work done. If usage is high, I would find out why, such as rework, waste or theft, and act on it.
markingPoints: Issues against the bill of materials and cutting list
Kits marked with job and assembly numbers
Issue notes signed, with bin cards updated
Consumables issued in controlled amounts; returns booked back
Compares issued with estimated and investigates high usage

essays.stem: Two days before a job is due to start, you find that the store is short of the 8 mm plate it needs. Explain what you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the facts: how much plate is needed, how much is in stock, and whether any is held for another job or as marked offcuts that could be used. Then I would tell purchasing at once and ask for the earliest delivery from the usual supplier and from other approved suppliers, with the grade and certificates the job needs. I would not change to a different thickness or grade on my own. If a substitute such as 10 mm plate is offered, I would ask the engineer or supervisor to approve it in writing, because a change can affect strength, weight, fit and the welding procedure. I would tell my manager and, if the date may slip, the client. Meanwhile I would re-plan the work so the team starts on parts that do not need the plate. When the plate arrives, I would check it and update the schedule, and I would review why the shortage was not found earlier.
markingPoints: Checks the facts, including other stock and usable offcuts
Tells purchasing at once and looks for approved sources
No substitute without written approval from the engineer or supervisor, with the reason
Informs the manager and client; re-plans work meanwhile
Checks the delivery and reviews why the shortage was missed

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can reduce material waste and scrap in a fabrication shop. Include how waste can be measured.
essays.modelAnswer: Waste can be measured by comparing the steel issued with the steel in the finished work. For example, if 1 200 kg is issued and the items contain 1 080 kg, 120 kg or 10% has been lost. Plate yield can be measured as the area of parts divided by the area of the sheet. To reduce waste, the team leader can plan cutting lists so parts come out of standard lengths with little left over, and nest plate parts closely. Offcuts should be marked with size and grade and kept in an offcut rack, and checked before new stock is cut. Accurate marking out and correct cutting settings reduce scrap from mistakes. Consumables are wasted less if they are issued in measured amounts, kept dry and used down to a short stub. Good storage stops rust and damage. Finally, sorted scrap should be sold for recycling. Results should be shared with the team each month.
markingPoints: Measures waste: issued versus used, or plate yield, with a worked example
Plans cutting lists and nesting to reduce offcuts
Marks, stores and reuses offcuts
Reduces rework through accurate marking and cutting; controls consumables
Good storage, sorted scrap for recycling, and sharing results

essays.stem: Explain how you would deal with surplus materials, offcuts and scrap at the end of a fabrication job.
essays.modelAnswer: At the end of the job I would gather all unused materials from the work area. Full lengths, sheets and unopened consumables would be checked for damage, booked back into the store against the job and put back in their proper places, so stock records stay right. Useful offcuts would be marked with size, grade and heat number where needed, and stored on the offcut rack. Opened low-hydrogen electrodes would be returned to the oven or dealt with as the maker says. Material bought specially for the client might belong to the client, so I would check the contract and offer it to them. Scrap would be sorted into carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium, kept apart from rubbish, and sold to a recycler. Waste paint, thinners and rags would be stored safely and disposed of as the rules say. Finally, I would compare the material used with the estimate and report the result.
markingPoints: Gathers and checks unused materials and books them back into stock
Marks and stores useful offcuts
Handles opened consumables as the maker says
Checks whether surplus belongs to the client
Sorts scrap for recycling, disposes of hazardous waste correctly, and reports usage

essays.stem: Describe what a weekly materials status report to the workshop manager should contain, and explain how it helps the jobs run smoothly.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should be short, written and the same each week. For each job it should show the materials due that week and whether they have arrived, any late or short deliveries with the new date, and any items rejected for damage, wrong size or missing certificates. It should list shortages expected in the next two weeks and the action being taken, such as a new order or a substitute waiting for the engineer's approval. It should give stock levels of common items that are near their reorder point. It should compare the materials used so far with the estimate, and note any waste or loss found, such as a stocktake difference. Finally, it should list decisions needed from the manager. The report helps because problems are seen early, while there is still time to fix them, the manager can plan labour and promise dates with confidence, and costs are controlled before they run away.
markingPoints: Deliveries due, arrived, late or rejected
Expected shortages and actions
Stock levels near reorder point
Usage against estimate and any losses
Decisions needed, and explains how early warning helps planning and cost control

practical1.title: Bill of materials, cutting plan and materials schedule for a fabricated stand, with a store check
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a drawing of a small fabricated item (for example a tank stand or a workbench frame), a job programme and the store's bin cards. Share the roles: two members prepare the bill of materials (every part with section, size, grade and number off, plus bolts, consumables and paint), one prepares the cutting plan for the bar and the nesting sketch for the plate and works out the yield, one prepares the materials schedule (when each item must be in the shop, allowing for the lead times given), and one leads the store check. Then the whole group checks the store: count the stock of the items needed, compare the count with the bin cards, note any differences and mark the shortages. Finish by writing the requisitions for the shortages and a short status note to the workshop manager. In a group of four, the store-check lead also writes the status note. Every member signs their own part. Photograph each stage.
materials: Drawing, job programme, lead-time list and bin cards (from the assessor)
Access to the Centre's steel rack and consumables store
Squared paper, calculators, rulers and pens
Bill of materials, cutting plan, materials schedule, stock check, requisition and status note templates
Gloves and safety boots for the store check
photos: The cutting plan and plate nesting sketch with the yield worked out
The group counting stock on the rack and in the consumables store
The stock check sheet showing counts, bin card balances and differences
The requisitions and the status note
checklist: Read the drawing correctly and listed every part with the right section, size, grade and quantity
Planned cuts from standard lengths sensibly and worked out the yield correctly
Set realistic arrival dates from the programme and lead times
Counted stock carefully and recorded differences against the bin cards
Identified the shortages and wrote clear requisitions
Wrote or helped write a clear, short status note
Worked safely in the store (gloves, boots, no climbing racks) and left it tidy
safety: Wear gloves and safety boots in the steel rack; steel ends are sharp and heavy
Do not climb racks or pull lengths out alone; ask for help
Do not open sealed consumables packs; count them as they are

practical2.title: Receive, mark, store and issue materials for a coded job, keeping traceability
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a 'delivery' for a job that needs traceability: a few lengths of bar or section and some plate marked with heat numbers, the matching mill certificates (one with a planted error), a box of low-hydrogen electrodes, MIG wire and a delivery note with one planted mistake. Part 1: check the delivery against the delivery note, the order and the certificates, and record what is wrong. Part 2: mark each item with the job number and heat number, and store it correctly: on the rack apart from general stock, electrodes into the holding oven, wire in the dry store. Part 3: cut one length into two pieces, transferring the marks to both pieces before cutting, and return the offcut to the rack. Part 4: issue a kit to a 'welder' (one member) with a signed issue note, and update the bin cards. Part 5: write a traceability record linking each piece to its certificate. Share the parts so every member checks, marks, handles and records at least once. Photograph each stage.
materials: Steel bar or section and plate marked with heat numbers, mill certificates and a delivery note (from the assessor)
Low-hydrogen electrodes, a spool of MIG wire and access to the electrode holding oven
Paint markers, chalk and a measuring tape
Band saw or cold saw used under the Centre's rules
Issue notes, bin cards, receiving record and traceability record templates
Gloves, safety glasses, boots and ear protection
photos: The delivery being checked against the delivery note and certificates, with the errors marked
Each item marked with the job and heat numbers
The materials stored on the rack and in the oven and dry store
The marks transferred to both pieces before cutting, then the cut pieces and offcut
The signed issue note and updated bin cards
checklist: Checked the delivery fully and found the planted errors
Matched heat numbers to the certificates and recorded the results
Marked every item clearly with the job and heat numbers
Stored each material correctly and apart from general stock
Transferred marks before cutting and returned the marked offcut
Issued the kit with a correct, signed issue note and updated the bin cards
Handled steel safely with gloves and team lifts, and used the saw as the Centre allows
safety: Lift long lengths with two people or a lifting aid; wear gloves and boots
Use the saw only with its guards in place and as the Centre's rules allow
Use oven gloves or follow the maker's instructions when loading the electrode oven
Keep the receiving area clear and stack nothing higher than the rack allows
